learningObjectives.title: Learning theories of criminality (operant conditioning and social learning)
Eysenck's biological theory of the criminal personality
The effects of punishment and rehabilitation
Key studies: Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961) and Charlton et al. (2000)

questions.q: Who conducted the classic 1961 'Bobo doll' study into the imitation of aggression?
questions.explain: The Bobo doll study of aggression was carried out by Bandura, Ross and Ross in 1961.

questions.q: How many children took part in Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961)?
questions.explain: The study used 72 nursery-aged children, split equally between boys and girls.

questions.q: Which finding best describes the results of Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961)?
options: Boys imitated more physical aggression than girls, especially from a same-sex model
Girls were consistently more physically aggressive than boys
Children only imitated verbal aggression, never physical aggression
Children in every condition behaved identically
questions.explain: Children copied the aggressive model, with boys showing more physical aggression and imitation being stronger from a same-sex model.

questions.q: In Charlton et al. (2000), the behaviour of children was studied on which island?
questions.explain: Charlton et al. studied children on the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena.

questions.q: What was introduced to the island in 1995 in Charlton et al.'s (2000) natural experiment?
questions.explain: The study examined children's behaviour before and after television was first introduced in 1995.

questions.q: What did Charlton et al. (2000) conclude about the effect of introducing television?
options: There was no significant increase in aggressive or antisocial behaviour
Children became far more aggressive within weeks
Only girls showed a sharp rise in aggression
questions.explain: They found no significant increase in aggression after television arrived, challenging simple media-effects claims.

questions.q: Operant conditioning, used to explain how criminal behaviour is reinforced, is most associated with which psychologist?
questions.explain: Skinner developed operant conditioning, which explains how behaviour is shaped by reinforcement and punishment.

questions.q: In operant conditioning, positive reinforcement makes a behaviour:
options: More likely to be repeated because it is followed by a reward
Less likely because it is followed by punishment
questions.explain: Positive reinforcement adds a reward after a behaviour, increasing the chance it will be repeated.

questions.q: Social learning theory, which explains criminality through observation and imitation, was proposed by:
questions.explain: Bandura's social learning theory states that behaviour can be learned by observing and imitating models.

questions.q: In social learning theory, 'vicarious reinforcement' means a person is more likely to imitate a behaviour when they:
options: See the model being rewarded for that behaviour
Have a reactive autonomic nervous system
Are alone with no model present
questions.explain: Vicarious reinforcement is learning through seeing a model rewarded, which increases the likelihood of imitation.

questions.q: Leah watches her older sister get praised by friends for shoplifting, and later shoplifts herself. Which concept best explains Leah's behaviour?
questions.explain: Leah imitates the behaviour because she saw her sister rewarded for it, an example of vicarious reinforcement.

questions.q: A boy pays attention to a footballer, remembers his moves, copies them and is motivated by wanting to be like him. These steps are the mediational processes of:
questions.explain: Attention, retention, reproduction and motivation are the mediational processes in Bandura's social learning theory.

questions.q: Eysenck's theory of the criminal personality is based on which three dimensions?
questions.explain: Eysenck proposed that the criminal personality scores highly on extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism.

questions.q: According to Eysenck, extraverts are more likely to seek stimulation and take risks because they have:
options: No autonomic nervous system at all
questions.explain: Eysenck argued extraverts have an under-aroused nervous system, so they seek excitement and stimulation.

questions.q: Eysenck argued that people high in neuroticism are harder to socialise partly because they have:
options: A reactive, unstable autonomic nervous system
A calm, highly stable nervous system
questions.explain: High neuroticism involves a reactive, unstable autonomic nervous system, making conditioning to social rules more difficult.

questions.q: A key assumption of Eysenck's personality theory is that personality is:
questions.explain: Eysenck's theory is biological, proposing that personality has a strong genetic and inherited basis.

questions.q: An offender scores highly on extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism. According to Eysenck, this makes the person:
options: More likely to show the criminal personality
Less likely than average to offend
Immune to the effects of reinforcement
questions.explain: High scores on all three dimensions fit Eysenck's profile of the criminal personality.

questions.q: A token economy in a prison is regarded as a form of operant conditioning because it:
options: Reinforces desired behaviour with rewards that can be exchanged for privileges
Relies on inmates observing and imitating staff
Is based on inherited personality traits
questions.explain: Token economies use positive reinforcement, giving tokens for good behaviour that are exchanged for rewards.

questions.q: A main aim of rehabilitation, compared with punishment, is to:
options: Increase the length of prison sentences
questions.explain: Rehabilitation focuses on changing offenders' behaviour to lower the chance they reoffend.

questions.q: In a young offenders' institution, inmates earn tokens for good behaviour which they swap for extra privileges. This rehabilitation method is called:
questions.explain: Earning exchangeable tokens for good behaviour is the defining feature of a token economy programme.
